States and diagrams

Dome computes the properties of a state from two independent properties, with h, u and s measured from each fluid's stated reference state. This page follows the second example, Help › Examples › States and properties (water).

Agreement with the tables

Enthalpy, internal energy and entropy are shifted to named reference states: the steam tables' for water, each refrigerant's own tables', h = 0 at 0 K for air and the other ideal gases. Differences between states, and the cycle results built from them, agree closely with the tables; a single value can differ from the printed table by about 1 kJ/kg, and by up to about 5 kJ/kg in parts of the superheated tables. These differences come from the equations behind each: Dome uses CoolProp's current reference equations, and the printed tables were computed from earlier ones.

R-134a's differences matter most, because its differences between states are small. Dome's R-134a is the international standard equation (Tillner-Roth and Baehr, 1994), from which NIST's published values also come; the textbook's R-134a tables were computed from an earlier equation (Wilson and Basu, 1988). Saturated vapor runs 0.7 to 1.2 kJ/kg above the saturation table from −40 to 48 °C; superheated vapor runs lower as the temperature rises, by about 1 kJ/kg at 60 °C, 2 at 100 °C and up to 4.7 kJ/kg at 200 °C; saturated liquid runs low below −10 °C, by up to 2.1 kJ/kg at −40 °C. A heat or work found between a saturated state and a hot superheated one can therefore differ from the tables' answer by several percent: 4 % for a rigid tank of R-134a cooled from 100 °C to saturated vapor at 20 °C. Propane runs up to 2.6 kJ/kg below its tables near its critical point, and up to 1.7 kJ/kg below them in superheated vapor above 100 °C.

Fluids

A fluid line sets the fluid for the state lines after it: water, r134a, r22, ammonia, propane or air. Air is an ideal gas with variable specific heats, h = 0 at 0 K. A state of another fluid names it in parentheses: state 2 (r134a) : ….

Five other gases are ideal gases in the same way, from 220 to 3250 K: nitrogen (or n2), oxygen (o2), carbondioxide (co2), carbonmonoxide (co) and water_ig (h2o_ig), water vapor as an ideal gas. Their h, u and s are per unit mass, so h(n2, T = 298 [K], p = 1 [atm]) * M(n2) is the molar enthalpy h̄, which agrees with the printed molar table to within about 6 kJ/kmol. water_ig counts h from 0 K, as the other ideal gases do, not on the steam tables: its h differs from that of water (or h2o) by a constant, so the two are not mixed in one balance, and an equation where they meet is an error (see moist air below).

State lines

fluid water
p_b = 15 [bar]
state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C]
state 2 : p = p_b, x = 0.3
state 3 : p = p_b, h = 2200 [kJ/kg]
state 4 : p = p_b, T = T_4
  • state L : a = …, b = … fixes state L from two of p, T, v, u, h, s and x, and defines p_L, T_L, v_L, u_L, h_L, s_L and x_L. A label may be a number or a name such as 2s.
  • The two values may be numbers, variables or expressions, and may be unknowns found by the rest of the sheet.
  • A pair that does not fix a state is refused with the reason: values outside the property data, p and T together on the saturation line, and pairs that fit more than one state.

Property functions

A property function gives one property at a state that need not be numbered: h(water, p = p_b, x = 0). The functions are p, T, v, u, h, s, x, cp, cv and rho, and Tsat(water, p = …) and psat(water, T = …) give saturation values. M(water) is a fluid's molar mass. Unknowns may sit inside them. Each input has the units of its property and is checked as a state line's property is: in h(water, T = T_x, x = 0) = 100 [kJ/kg], T_x is a temperature, shown in °C, and h(water, T = 300, x = 0) needs a unit after the 300. An unknown that has units only as an input starts from its name, as a variable without units does, since its units say nothing of where its value lies: a wet bulb lies below the dry bulb.

Moist air

p = 1.013 [bar]
T_1 = 30 [C]; phi_1 = 0.5
omega_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
T_dp1 = Tdp(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
  • A moist-air state is fixed by p and two other properties, so moist air (moistair, or humidair) has property functions and no state lines. Each takes exactly three named properties, one of them p.
  • The functions are omega (humidity ratio, kg of vapor per kg of dry air), phi (relative humidity, a fraction from 0 to 1), T, Twb (wet-bulb temperature), Tdp (dew point), pv (partial pressure of the vapor), and h, v, s and cp per kg of dry air.
  • The inputs are p with T and any one of phi, omega, Twb, Tdp, pv or h, or one of the pairs phi and Twb, phi and pv, phi and h, omega and Twb, omega and h, Twb and Tdp, Tdp and h. Other pairs are refused with this list.
  • The properties come from CoolProp's humid-air model, a real mixture: humidity ratios near room conditions are about 0.5 % above those of the ideal-gas relations, and pv is about 0.4 % above phi pg. The enthalpy of dry air is zero at the psychrometric datum: 0 °C on an SI sheet, and 0 °F on a sheet in English units, so there h(moistair, p = 14.696 [psi], T = 80 [F], phi = 0.5) is 31.25 Btu/lb, against 0.24 × 80 + omega hg = 31.18 with hg from the steam tables; and the water in the moist air is on the reference of Dome's water states, so a condensate's h(water, T = …, x = 0) enters a balance directly.
  • A state with more water vapor than saturated air holds at its temperature, such as T = 25 °C with omega = 0.05, or a mixture of two streams that would form fog, is refused for every property, and the message says the limit it is past, such as the most vapor the air holds at that temperature. An unknown inside a moist-air function whose equation holds only at such a state has no value: with h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_2, omega = w_1) and h_2 below the h of saturated air at w_1, the air is cooled past its dew point at constant omega, and the message gives that lowest h and the dew point, below which some of the water vapor condenses.
  • Each fluid's h, u and s are measured from a reference of its own, and Dome carries the reference through the equations as it carries units. Water is on the steam tables; each refrigerant on its own tables; air (h(air, …), a state of air) and the other ideal gases count from 0 K, and so does a heat capacity times a value that is certainly a temperature, such as cp_a*T_1 with T_1 = 30 [C], or cp_a*(T_1 - 273.15 [K]), whose T_1 - 273.15 [K] is a temperature 273.15 K below T_1; moist air counts its dry air from 0 °C (0 °F in English units) and its water on the steam tables. A difference of temperatures carries no reference, as in cp_a*(T_1 - T_0), nor a heat capacity times a temperature given in [K], which may be a change, such as a condenser's m_w*c_w*T_rise with T_rise = 10 [K]. An unknown h, or one typed from a table, takes from its equation only the reference the equation still requires: in m_a*h_a1 + m_w*h_w1 = m_a*h_a2 + m_w*h_w2 with the air from h(air, …), h_w2 takes the steam tables', so T(water, h = h_w2, p = 1 [bar]) reads it. A heat or a work never supplies a reference to close a balance. A property function that reads a variable as its h gives it that fluid's reference first. References belong to substances: an equation that takes water from both the steam tables and water_ig, or dry air from both h(air, …) and moist air, is an error, whatever the amounts.
  • A sum carries both of its operands' references, a product keeps them, and a difference of two values on one reference carries none; the operands of a difference are all that a chain of sums and differences adds and all that it subtracts. An equation or a difference whose two sides are on different references, neither of them none, is an error on its line, and so is an h given to a property function on another reference. So every stream is written one way: every stream with h(moistair, …), or every stream with the ideal-gas form cp_a*(T - T_0) + omega*h(water, T = …, x = 1), which carries the steam tables' reference alone, or every stream with h(air, …) + omega*h(water, …). Dry air at 30 °C mixed at 1 atm with moist air at 10 °C and phi = 0.8, each stream carrying 1 kg/s of dry air, gives 19.9 °C written h(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], omega = 0); written h(air, T = 30 [C], p = p), dry air at 0 °C has h of about 273 kJ/kg on air's ideal-gas reference, the mixture would be at 154 °C, and the balance is an error. The ideal-gas form beside h(moistair, …) in a difference such as q = h_2 - h_1, or read by T(moistair, …, h = …), is an error whose message says to write every stream one way. A dehumidifier written with the vapor from h(water_ig, …) and the condensate from h(water, T = T_2, x = 0) is an error that names the vapor's h as hv = hg(T) on the steam tables; written with h(water, T = …, x = 1) for the vapor, it gives 41.79 kJ per kg of dry air.
  • The wet-bulb temperature is taken over liquid water when it lies above the triple point of water (0.01 °C) and over ice otherwise, so a state near 0 °C has one wet bulb, and a wet bulb given is read the same way; where the state also has the other, a warning on the line names both. Dry air (omega = 0) has no dew point.
  • Variables named phi, omega, pv, Twb or Tdp are still variables; only a name followed by an opening parenthesis is a function.

The states table

The States tab of the results lists the phase and properties of every state in the units chosen in the header. The two properties given on each state line are in bold. The copy button at the right of the tab's header copies the table as tab-separated text, and File › Export › States table writes it as a CSV file.

Diagrams

A plot line draws a property diagram of states of the sheet: Ts, Tv, pv, ph or hs. The T–v and p–v diagrams have v on a logarithmic axis. Between two state labels, a path names the property held constant.

PathProcess
-p-, -s-, -T-, -v-, -h-At constant pressure, entropy, temperature, specific volume or enthalpy. Drawn dashed when that property differs between the two states, as for an expansion with a turbine efficiency.
--A straight line.
 
plot Ts : 1 -p- 2 -p- 3 -p- 4
plot ph : 1 -p- 2 -p- 3 -p- 4

Each plot line is one figure, with its own tab in the figure pane. The buttons in the pane's header zoom to a box, fit the view to the data, show data tips and export the figure. The boxes under the figure show or hide the previous run, the saturation dome, and the isobars or isotherms. The isobars run through the dome, flat where the fluid is two-phase, and those at the pressures of the figure's states are drawn darker and labelled with their values, so each isobaric process lies on a labelled line; on p–v and p–h diagrams the same holds for isotherms.

Dragging a state

A state can be dragged along an axis of the figure when the property it is given on that axis is an input of the sheet. An input is a line name = number [unit], or a number written in a state line (x = 0 in state 3 makes x_3 an input), so T = T_4 with T_4 = 320 [C] qualifies, and so does T = 320 [C] written in the state line. A ring marks each such state. The axes hold still while the state is dragged, and the value moves by as much as the pointer moves from where the drag began; a state dragged to the edge of the plot stops there, and the axes fit the data again on release. The new value is written where the number stands, and the sheet is solved again.

The previous run

After a line is edited, Dome shows what changed: the edited line is tinted and shows the previous value of an input, values that changed show the change beside them, the changed variables and states are tinted in the Workspace and the states table, and figures draw the previous run dashed with a legend naming the change. The previous run is the run from before the edit of the line began: the edit ends when the cursor leaves the line, on Enter, when the sheet loses focus, or after 10 seconds without typing, so a pause in the middle of a line does not replace it. A line added that leaves the figure as it was, such as a check line, draws no previous run. Below, the boiler pressure p_b of the second example was changed from 15 bar to 30 bar.
